## Understanding the problem
`numWays[i]` (1-indexed) is the number of unordered ways to make amount i with unlimited coins of unknown denominations ≤ n. Recover any valid denomination set, sorted, or [].

In example 1, amount 1 has 0 ways so 1 isn't a coin; amount 2 jumps by exactly 1, so 2 is a coin; pattern continues with 4 and 6. Example 3 fails because amount 3 would need 3 ways but {1,2} gives only 2 and adding 3 would overshoot.

Key fact: adding denomination i increases ways(i) by exactly 1 (the single-coin way [i]), since all other ways for amount i use smaller coins. So processing amounts in order, the discrepancy at each amount must be 0 or 1.
k: Adding coin i contributes exactly one new way to amount i, namely [i] itself.
Process amounts ascending, maintaining the unbounded-knapsack ways array with coins chosen so far; a discrepancy of 0 means no coin, 1 means coin i, anything else is impossible.
Simulation is O(n²), trivially fast for n ≤ 100.

a.i: Maintain cur[a] = ways to make amount a using confirmed coins (< current i). At amount i, if cur[i] matches numWays[i-1], coin i is absent; if it's one less, coin i is present — add it and propagate cur[j] += cur[j-i]; otherwise no set exists.
s: For i = 1..n: if cur[i] == numWays[i-1], continue; else if cur[i] + 1 == numWays[i-1], append i and for j = i..n do cur[j] += cur[j-i]; else return [].
a.t: O(n²) — for each candidate coin we sweep the ways array once.

w: Use 64-bit intermediates since ways can reach 2·10⁸ and sums overflow 32-bit in C++/Java. Pitfall: forgetting that the +1 comes only from the single-coin way, or updating cur before comparing. Follow-up: recover denominations when numWays counts ordered sequences (compositions) instead.
